text.p: Russian President Boris Yeltsin was back in hospital on Thursday, with the first signs of pneumonia, renewing doubts about his ability to govern his vast country just two months after heart surgery.

Yeltsin, 65, was in "a quite satisfactory" condition after being taken to hospital on Wednesday evening on doctors' orders, said the surgeon who led the quintuple heart bypass operation on him on November 5.
Renat Akchurin told reporters he had not seen the president, who returned to work on December 23 after almost six months off with heart problems, but said he had spoken to the doctors treating him.
"As far as I know, Yeltsin's health is quite satisfactory, and he is receiving regular medication," he said, adding the doctors said the illness was flu and unrelated to the surgery.
"The post-operative period finished a month ago, so it seems to me that it makes no sense to now connect something with the operation."
Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin, Yeltsin's constitutional number two, was reported to have begun a short break on Thursday but was keeping a close eye on developments.

"The head of the Russian government Viktor Chernomyrdin, on a short holiday which he is spending near Moscow, is controlling the situation and maintaining close ties with us," Interfax quoted first deputy prime minister Alexei Bolshakov saying.

Under the constitution, Chernomyrdin would stand in for up to three months before an election if Yeltsin was unable to govern the nuclear state of 150 million people. He stepped in for a day when Yeltsin had his heart bypass.

Yeltsin was looking pale and tired and had cancelled all appointments since Monday because of what the Kremlin said then was a heavy cold. He had been resting in a residence just outside Moscow since Monday.
On Wednesday evening, the Kremlin said doctors had detected early signs of pneumonia when they examined the president.

"In connection with this, in order to make a better diagnosis and to conduct appropriate treatment, a decision has been taken to take him to the Central Clinical Hospital (in Moscow) for several days," said a Kremlin statement.

A presidential spokesman said Yeltsin entered the hospital at about nine p.m. (1800 GMT) on Wednesday. The spokesman made no mention of the trigger which controls Russia's nuclear arsenal but it usually accompanies Yeltsin at all times.
The Kremlin announced Yeltsin's new illness quickly after doctors ordered him to hospital, but it has not always revelaed the full truth about the president's condition in the past.

Pioneering U.S. heart surgeon Michael DeBakey, an adviser to Akchurin and the other doctors who carried out the heart operation on Yeltsin, said he expected the president to make a quick recovery from what he also said was probably flu.
Asked if Yeltsin had recovered from the trauma of the heart surgery, DeBakey said: "I would say pretty much yes and his heart is functioning now virtually normally."
But some of Yeltsin's political opponents seized on his new health problem to attack him.

General Alexander Lebed, sacked by Yeltsin as national security adviser last October for manifesting open presidential ambitions, said on Thursday the president's illness had left Russia rudderless and that he should step down.

"The president is badly ill. It's a difficult age, he's had a difficult operation, a not entirely healthy way of life for the past 40 years. It doesn't leave much hope," said the growling general, who would be a strong presidential candidate.

"(Yeltsin) should offer his resignation. The president is in hospital, the prime minister is on holiday and people have not been paid and are not paid. No one has dealt with the economy ...Someone has to answer for that, someone has to rule."
Yeltsin suffered two heart attacks in 1995 and spent much of last year out of the Kremlin.

His long absences fuelled a struggle for position among Kremlin officials that culminated in Lebed's sacking. Economic problems also mounted, including tax evasion which drained state coffers and led to long delays in wage and pension payments.
Yeltsin vowed to deal with those issues immediately on his return to work but did not have time to do so.

Yeltsin, who played a major role in ending communist rule and overseeing economic reforms, has been president since 1991. He fought a tough re-election campaign last year but fell ill just before the decisive round of voting on July 3.
